summary: Updates RFC 2418 to give working group chairs explicit responsibility for managing their mailing lists. In particular, chairs may temporarily suspend the posting privileges of disruptive individuals. It was replaced by RFC 9945.

plainLanguage.summary: The person in charge of a club can tell someone who keeps shouting to take a short break from the group chat. This memo gives chairs that power.

questions: can a wg chair suspend posting privileges
subtitle: Lets IETF working group chairs suspend a disruptive person's list posting for up to 30 days.

tldr.problem: RFC 2418 gave chairs authority to manage disruption in meetings, but suspending someone's mailing list posting privileges needed full IESG approval.
tldr.mechanism: It replaces the last paragraph of RFC 2418 section 3.2, letting a chair suspend posting privileges for no more than 30 days as a last resort, after warnings and consulting the Area Director.

today: RFC 3934 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 94) that has been obsoleted by RFC 9945. It updated RFC 2418.

sections.title: The Gap in RFC 2418
sections.content:
RFC 2418 gave working group (WG) chairs more authority over face-to-face discussions than over mailing list discussions. In meetings, a chair can refuse to grant the floor to anyone who is unprepared, covering inappropriate material, or in the chair's opinion disrupting the WG process.

For a mailing list, RFC 2418 did not give the chair authority to suspend an individual's posting privileges, and explicitly required full IESG approval for that action. RFC 3934 updates section 3.2 of RFC 2418 so chairs can temporarily suspend posting privileges without IESG approval.
sections.plainLanguage: A teacher could tell a noisy kid to stop talking in class, but could not do the same in the class chat. This fixes that.

sections.title: The Escalation Steps
sections.content:
The replacement text lays out steps. Unless the behavior is severe enough that it must be stopped immediately, the chair should first try to discourage it by communicating directly with the individual. If it persists, the chair should send at least one public warning on the WG list.

As a last resort, typically after one or more explicit warnings and consultation with the responsible Area Director, the chair may suspend posting privileges for not more than 30 days. The person must still be able to receive messages posted to the list. Like all other chair decisions, a suspension is subject to appeal as described in RFC 2026.
sections.plainLanguage: First the chair asks nicely, then warns in public, and only then pauses the person's posting for a short time. The person can still read what others write.

sections.title: Limits of the Mechanism
sections.content:
The mechanism is meant for short suspensions only. It does not let a chair suspend privileges for more than 30 days, whatever the type or severity of the incident. Further disruption by the same person is considered separately and may bring further warnings or suspensions.

Longer suspensions and other methods of list control must follow other IETF-approved procedures. The RFC points to BCP 83 (RFC 3683) as one set already accepted by the community. Its Security Considerations section says the change affects process only and has no security considerations.
sections.plainLanguage: A chair can only give a short time-out. Anything longer needs a different, bigger process.

references.text: Bradner, S., "IETF Working Group Guidelines and Procedures", BCP 25, RFC 2418, September 1998.
Bradner, S., "The Internet Standards Process -- Revision 3", BCP 9, RFC 2026, October 1996.
